Flooding Along Loire River Disrupts French Construction Materials Industry

Heavy rainfall and swelling rivers have brought significant flooding to the Loire Valley this week, causing widespread disruption across the construction materials industry in central France. Key production sites, quarries, and transport routes remain impacted, with company officials warning of potential delays in deliveries and temporary stoppages at several plants.

The Loire River burst its banks in several locations between Tours and Orléans following days of intense rain. Water levels reached a 15-year high on Tuesday night, inundating access roads and rail lines that serve many of the region’s industrial zones.

Cie de Saint-Gobain SA, a major player in the sector, confirmed that operations at its Blois plasterboard and insulation facility have been partially suspended since Monday evening due to flooding of nearby supply roads. “Our teams are working around the clock to ensure staff safety and minimize production downtime,” said site manager Laurent Dubois. “However, several key suppliers are unable to reach the plant, and outbound deliveries are delayed until water levels recede.”

Other companies, including regional aggregates producer Matériaux du Val, also reported interruptions at their sand and gravel quarries along the river. “We have halted extraction at two sites near Amboise due to rising groundwater and access difficulties,” said managing director Claire Lefevre. “Every day the quarries are closed costs us thousands of euros, and our clients are facing shortages of essential materials.”

The French Construction Materials Association estimates that nearly 18 percent of the region’s concrete plants and aggregates sites are directly affected by the floods as of Wednesday afternoon. “This is a critical corridor for the supply of materials to construction projects in western and central France,” explained association spokesperson Julien Marceau. “With major highways like the D952 under water, lorry traffic is severely disrupted, and rail freight is also experiencing delays.”

Union representatives have expressed concerns for workers’ safety, especially for those involved in emergency maintenance or clean-up operations. “We urge all employers to prioritize safety and follow local authorities’ instructions,” said Isabelle Girard, a regional union official.

With more rain forecast for the coming days, industry analysts are warning of extended disruptions and possible knock-on effects for construction projects dependent on timely deliveries. Local officials said they are monitoring river levels closely and coordinating with emergency services.
